new_en: Seif katan 3, "and born," etc. One must examine him afterward, because perhaps when the organ becomes erect he will appear as one born without a visible foreskin. If so, although at present, when it is not erect, he does not appear that way, he is nevertheless considered one born in that state, and hatafat dam brit does not override Shabbos.

"And born without a visible foreskin." I found written that it requires study why nowadays the custom is not to examine the child afterward. One must say as Bach writes in Yoreh De'ah, siman 264, that he must appear without a visible foreskin even when the organ is not erect. Accordingly, if he does not appear that way when it is not erect, the brit milah may be performed on Shabbos. This requires study whether one may rely upon this to permit an act involving the severe laws of Shabbos.

Seif katan 4, "2 foreskins," meaning 2 skins one above the other. I saw in Responsa Panim Meirot, part 2, end of siman 31, that he understood these 2 skins as referring to the skins involved in priyah. He therefore wrote that when 2 skins are seen one should not perform the priyah on Shabbos but should wait until after Shabbos. His wording implies that the priyah should be done on Sunday, since even a brit milah not performed at its proper time must be performed by day. Yet the priyah membrane is thin, and if one waits so long it may adhere strongly to the organ and become difficult or impossible to separate, potentially endangering the child or leaving him with an incomplete brit milah.

It therefore appears more correct, in my humble opinion, that "2 skins" means 2 upper foreskins that are ordinarily called skins, whereas the thin membrane separated during priyah is generally called a membrane, although at times it too is called a skin.

One may ask how it can be known before the procedure that there is another skin beneath the upper one. A case is possible where 1 foreskin covers the entire organ and has only the small urinary opening typical of infants, while a second foreskin lies above it and has a much larger opening toward the top. We indeed find infants with only 1 foreskin whose opening is unusually wide at the urinary opening, so that beneath it the organ appears as though there were no visible foreskin. In the case of 2 foreskins, there is 1 ordinary foreskin closed except at the urinary opening, and above it another skin covering the organ but opened widely near the head. In this way one can see that 2 distinct skins require cutting.

"Twilight." See Magen Avraham, who concludes that if the infant was born approximately a quarter-hour before nightfall the matter is doubtful, while if he was born earlier the brit milah is performed on Friday. If he was born on Shabbos approximately a quarter-hour before nightfall, the brit milah is performed on Shabbos according to this calculation.

Radbaz, siman 282, writes that if an infant was born on Friday after sunset but before 3 medium stars were visible, and there is doubt whether the birth occurred before the end of sunset or after it but before the stars appeared, the brit milah is deferred. See also the extensive discussion at the end of Darkei Noam in the treatise Milchamot Mitzvah, Responsa Bach siman 154, and the later authorities.

"Born without a visible foreskin." It requires study why the custom is not to examine afterward. Magen Avraham explains in the name of Bach, Yoreh De'ah siman 264, that the child must appear this way even when the organ is not erect. If he does not appear so in that state, one performs the brit milah on Shabbos. Magen Avraham nevertheless questions whether this is sufficient basis to permit an act involving severe Shabbos laws.

See also Shach at the end of Yoreh De'ah, siman 264, and siman 263 regarding a concealed foreskin. Where actual tissue obstructing the brit milah remains, the mitzvah can override Shabbos under the ordinary rules. Some authorities discuss the case of one born without a visible foreskin and indicate that the drawing of covenantal blood should preferably be done after Shabbos. The Talmud in Shabbos 135 is the principal source and the matter remains subject to the distinctions of the earlier authorities.

"Twilight." The calculation of twilight for brit milah follows the distinctions explained by the authorities concerning sunset and the appearance of 3 medium stars. If a child is born before the doubtful period, the eighth day is counted from that day; if the birth occurs during the doubtful period, the brit milah is deferred because a doubtful brit milah does not override Shabbos.

If the infant's head emerged before nightfall but the full birth occurred after nightfall, one must determine whether the head had emerged sufficiently to constitute birth. Where it is clear from the interval that the head emerged while it was still day, the halachic birth may be attributed to the earlier time. Where the timing is uncertain, one must be stringent.

If, after the full birth, 3 medium stars were seen, this alone does not prove that they were already visible when the head emerged. If only large stars had been visible before, they do not establish night. Where many small stars are already visible, there is stronger basis to treat it as night.

The authorities therefore rule that where there was a perceptible delay between emergence of the head and completion of birth, one cannot simply apply a presumption that the birth occurred only at the later moment. For Torah law, emergence of the head can itself constitute birth. The time of that emergence must therefore be evaluated independently, and if it remains doubtful the brit milah does not override Shabbos.

Seif 5, "and born without a visible foreskin." This follows Rabbah there, who says that we are concerned for a hidden foreskin, and the halacha follows Rabbah against Rav Yosef.

"And one born by Caesarean section, and a non-Jewish woman," etc., "and one," etc. The ruling remains doubtful because Rav Asi's position differs from the first Tanna. We are uncertain whether Rav Asi had heard the baraita and nevertheless disagreed with the first Tanna, or whether he had not heard the baraita and would have accepted it had he heard it.

"Twilight." See Mishnah Berurah, where I cited Radbaz. This is not treated as a classic double doubt, 1 doubt whether it was still day and another doubt within twilight itself. Pri Megadim suggests that perhaps the mother's prior status as pregnant is relevant, though that presumption is not especially strong for determining the precise halachic time of birth.

Where there is uncertainty whether the head emerged before or during twilight, one cannot automatically say that we establish the mother in her prior status until the later moment. Once the head emerged, the Torah may already regard the child as born. Thus, if a known interval elapsed between emergence of the head and completion of the birth, the timing of the head's emergence must itself be evaluated.

Several authorities discuss a case in which the child was fully born after 3 medium stars were visible, but there was a delay from the emergence of the head. If the witnesses can estimate that the head clearly emerged while it was still day, one follows what they saw. If they cannot determine the time, there is substantial reason to be stringent and not allow the brit milah to override Shabbos.

"Born without a visible foreskin." The term refers to a child who appears so even without erection. If the child appears to have a foreskin when the organ is not erect, but after erection it appears otherwise, the authorities discuss whether this status is considered present from birth. The practical law depends upon whether there is truly hidden foreskin tissue that requires cutting or merely hatafat dam brit.

"Caesarean section." A child removed through the abdominal wall rather than through ordinary birth does not have the same law concerning an eighth-day brit milah overriding Shabbos, because the Scriptural formulation connects the eighth day with the mother's status of birth impurity.

"2 foreskins." The authorities explain this either as 2 organs or as 2 superimposed foreskins. In either interpretation the brit milah does not override Shabbos because of the unresolved doubt concerning the Torah's application to the case.

The common denominator of these cases is uncertainty concerning whether the Torah's ordinary rule of an eighth-day brit milah applies in a form strong enough to override Shabbos. Where the mother's birth does not create tumat leidah, such as Caesarean delivery or a non-Jewish mother who converts only afterward, the exclusion follows the Scriptural relationship between the mother's impurity and the son's eighth day.
